Meta AI, the assistant built into WhatsApp, refused to make campaign material for Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva while making it for his rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, according to tests by a Folha de S.Paulo column. Meta says a temporary election-compliance block missed a prompt. Lula's campaign has taken the matter to the electoral court. This post separates what is reported, what Meta says, and what nobody has verified yet.

The short version: it is a single outlet's test plus company and court statements, so treat the "bias" framing as a claim under investigation, not a finding. But the case is a clean, concrete example of how a chatbot's safety filter can behave unevenly during an election, and it matters to anyone shipping or using AI image tools around political content.

## Quick answers

## What Folha reported, step by step

Folha's column reports that Meta AI refused a request for a poster carrying the phrase "Lula 13" (13 is the number of Lula's party, the PT) but fulfilled a request for one with "Flávio 22" (22 is Flávio Bolsonaro's party number, the PL). When asked about the difference, the chatbot reportedly acknowledged the inconsistency and attributed it to an automatic safety filter.

Folha then widened the test. Its correspondents in the United States, Argentina and Germany, using accounts without Brazilian area codes, were able to generate Lula posters, including ones with photos. Brazilian numbers, even when used abroad, had their requests blocked. If that holds up, the block is tied to the account's phone number region rather than where the person physically is, which fits a deliberate election-period rule applied to Brazilian users.

After Meta responded, Folha says the chatbot kept creating images that said "Vote Flávio" but refused "Vote Lula" and "Vote Luiz Inácio". That detail is important: Meta's explanation was that the system missed prompts using only the first name "Flávio". A fix aimed at that gap would be expected to remove the asymmetry, and Folha reports it had not, at least at the time of writing.

## What Meta says

Meta's statement to Folha, as quoted by the paper: "in compliance with Brazil's election rules, we have temporarily prohibited the recommendation of candidates or the generation of images of them." The company says the senator's material was produced because the filter did not recognise prompts that used only the name "Flávio", and that it took additional measures so such prompts are also covered. Meta denies the accusations and says it is committed to equal treatment.

That is a coherent explanation for a one-off miss, but it does not by itself explain why Lula prompts were blocked when phrased in several ways while Flávio ones kept working, which is the behavior Folha says it still saw. Only Meta's logs and the filter's rules can settle that, which is exactly what the court has asked for.

## The legal track: TSE and ANPD

According to Folha, Lula's campaign took the case to the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) on Wednesday, October 14. It had already said on Friday, October 10 that it would go to the court and to Brazil's data protection authority (ANPD) over alleged interference by Meta. The TSE ordered the company to provide technical explanations and preserve records.

This sits inside a broader dispute. Brazilian outlets such as Jornal do Brasil reported that the campaign also accused Meta of interfering through the shutdown of the president's ad account and interruptions in view and reach data on his official Instagram profile. The campaign's own note, quoted there, cites a series of unexplained technical problems and says the company's systems lack transparency. Those are separate claims about Instagram and ads, not about the WhatsApp chatbot, and nothing in the reporting shows they are linked.

## Why a "safety filter" can look like bias

Most consumer chatbots layer several systems: a model, an input classifier, and an output filter. Election rules add a fourth: a policy list of names, parties and numbers to be handled differently. Uneven results often come from the plain mechanics of that list.

- Name coverage. A list that includes full names and ballot numbers may miss a first name, a nickname or a party number. Meta's own explanation points at exactly this for "Flávio".

- Token and string matching. "Lula 13" is a distinctive string the filter can catch. A prompt built only of a given name plus a number may slip through.

- Different strictness by language or locale. Folha's finding that foreign phone numbers get through suggests region gating rather than model behaviour.

- Self-reports are unreliable. The chatbot saying it was "an automatic safety filter" is the model narrating, not an audit. Treat it as a lead, not evidence.

None of this proves innocence or intent. It shows why neutral enforcement needs testing with both sides' names, nicknames, numbers and slogans, and why launching an election restriction without that test invites precisely this story.

## What is confirmed and what is not

## What this means for builders and users

If you ship an assistant or image generator that touches politics, a few practical lessons come out of this:

- Test symmetry before launch. Run the same prompt template across every candidate, party number, slogan and nickname, in each language you support, and log the refusal rates side by side.

- Don't key restrictions only to phone region. It is easy to bypass and creates the appearance of selective enforcement, as Folha's cross-border tests show.

- Keep audit logs. The TSE's order to preserve records shows regulators will ask. Without per-request filter decisions you cannot demonstrate neutrality.

- Explain refusals in plain language. A refusal that says "election rules" for everyone reads differently from a silent block on one name.

- Don't let the model explain itself. Log the policy rule that fired instead of asking the chatbot why it refused.

For readers who use AI tools during an election: assume any political output may be filtered inconsistently, check claims against primary sources, and be wary of AI-made campaign material shared as if authentic. Teams deploying agents that act on political or public-facing content can look at AgentBeam , the agent security platform from the explainx.ai team, which stops AI agents before they take dangerous actions.

## How it fits Meta's wider AI push

Meta AI is no longer a side feature. The company has been pushing Muse, its personal agent, across apps and devices, and we have covered the launch, the pricing, and the safety questions in depth. See our verdict on whether Muse is safe , the Muse Spark 1.3 launch and pricing , the Meta One subscription tiers , and the investigation into Muse and contact dossiers . The more an assistant is embedded in a chat app used by most of a country, the more its moderation choices become matters of public record and, as here, election law.

A related theme is how platforms steer attention with AI. Our post on Facebook's AI feed controls covers Meta's move to let users shape LLM-ranked feeds, and the earlier claim-versus-fact check on a viral Claude rumor shows the approach we apply here: attribute the claim, list what is checked, and say what is not.

## What to watch next

- Meta's technical response to the TSE. Whether it shares the filter rules, logs, and the date the restriction was introduced.

- A fresh independent test. If other outlets or researchers repeat the prompts with both candidates and publish the results, the asymmetry either reproduces or does not.

- Any ANPD step. The data protection authority was named by Lula's campaign; any action would add a privacy angle.

- Rules for AI in campaigns. The case may feed the debate over how electoral law treats generated campaign material and who is responsible for it.

We will update this post if the court or Meta publishes details.

## Bottom line

The verified part is narrow: a Brazilian newspaper's tests, a Meta statement about a temporary election rule, and a court order for explanations. The unverified part is the one drawing attention: whether the asymmetry was an accident of a name list or something more. Until the TSE process or independent tests say otherwise, the honest position is that Meta AI behaved unevenly in a high-stakes setting, the company says it was a filter gap, and the evidence for intent has not been presented.

Details are accurate as of October 15, 2026, based on Folha de S.Paulo and Brazilian press reports; the situation is moving and Meta may have changed the filter since.

https://explainx.ai/blog/modular-max-sou.markdown:
On October 22, 2026 Modular shipped MAX 26.7 and opened up the last big pieces of its inference stack. Social posts summarizing the release, attributed to Chris Lattner, Modular's co-founder, described Mojo and MAX as "fully open - for development, extension, and commercial use" (we could not open the original post). The company's own blog says something narrower: "MAX is now source available and open to everyone." Developers "can now explore, modify, and extend the entire MAX stack," including the graph compiler, runtime and hardware backends for CPUs and GPUs.

The gap between "fully open" and "source available" matters if you plan to build a product on it. This post sets the claim against the license text in Modular's public repository, so you know what is confirmed, what you can do, and what to read before committing.

## TL;DR: claim versus what the repo says

## What opened, according to Modular

Modular's blog post of October 22 says the release builds on earlier open kernels, models and serving infrastructure, and opens the "remaining core components that power MAX's heterogeneous capabilities: the graph compiler, runtime, and hardware backends." A companion post titled "Modular 26.7: Opening up MAX" accompanies it. The Modular blog is the primary source here; we could read its index summaries and the public repository but not the full posts, so read them yourself. The 26.7 summary calls the new MAX License "intentionally permissive" and says you can use, modify, extend and build commercial products with MAX without licensing fees or royalties, and that source for MAX plugins for other chips, including Qualcomm Dragonfly and Google TPU, is planned "in the coming months."

The modular/modular repository README gives a clear map of what is available and since when:

- Mojo compiler: since August 2026

- Mojo standard library: since March 2024

- MAX GPU programming abstractions and accelerator library (compute kernels): since May 2025

- MAX AI framework (model authoring in Python): since November 2025

- MAX graph compiler, runtime ( MLRT ), driver and model pipelines: listed as available now

The README also says "we're actively open-sourcing more of the Modular Platform over time," which tells you the staged approach continues. Our earlier post on the Mojo compiler going open source covers the first half of this story, and the AI chip architectures guide explains why a portable compiler and runtime matter across GPUs, TPUs and accelerators.

## What the MAX License actually says

This is the part the short posts skip. The repository's LICENSE states that Mojo and its contributions are under Apache 2.0 with LLVM Exceptions, while "portions of the MAX source code and its binary distribution are licensed under the MAX License," and the rest under Apache 2.0. The MAX License file is marked as last modified October 21, 2026, a day before the release, and names the licensor as "Modular Inc, a Qualcomm Company."

Key points from the license text, which we read directly:

- Grant. A perpetual, worldwide, non-exclusive, no-charge, royalty-free license to reproduce and prepare derivative works, distribute derivative works in object code, and use documentation internally. Section 1.1 calls it a "Limited Source License."

- Downstream terms. You may license your own derivative work under terms you choose, but any portion of MAX inside it stays under the MAX License, and you must include a human-readable copy of the terms.

- Applications. You may redistribute parts of MAX inside an application, in object code, provided the application has "material additional functionality beyond the included portions of MAX."

- Forks. Section 1.3 allows publishing modified source in a fork of Modular's repository to contribute to a Modular project. Distributing object code and applications stays governed by the grant above.

- No substitute built with AI. Section 1.4(d) says you shall not use MAX as training data, fine-tuning data, or input to any AI system to produce software that reimplements or substitutes for MAX. It adds that using AI tools to read, analyze, improve or explain MAX, or to build software that runs on or interoperates with MAX, is not restricted.

- Telemetry. Section 2.1 says use of MAX may involve collection of telemetry and usage data, which Modular and its affiliates may use "for any purpose", and that Modular owns it.

- Trademarks for hosted services. If you are a legal entity commercially deploying MAX as a hosted or managed AI training or inference service for other legal entities, you must use the Modular Accelerated mark under Modular's brand guidelines and get written approval for materials bearing it.

- Patents. A royalty-free patent license applies, ending if you file patent litigation alleging MAX infringes.

None of this makes MAX unusable. It does make "fully open" imprecise: by common definitions such as the Open Source Definition, a license that restricts what you may do with the code (here, the reimplementation and branding clauses) is source available rather than open source. Both statements are true in different senses, and the license file is what a lawyer will read.

## What this means if you build on it

If you run inference in-house. You can inspect and modify the compiler and runtime, and ship your own derivatives in compiled form. Read the telemetry section with your security team, because it applies to your use of MAX.

If you sell a hosted inference service. The trademark clause is the one to check. It does not forbid hosting, but it requires prominent Modular branding and approval workflows, which many providers would treat as a business term.

If you ship an app. Embedding runtime pieces is allowed when your app has substantial functionality of its own, in object code with the license copy included.

If you work on a competing runtime. Do not feed MAX source to a model to produce a lookalike. The clause is explicit, and the exception for interoperability is narrow.

If you work on kernels in Mojo. The compiler and standard library remain Apache 2.0, a much simpler position. The README notes that a single Bazel command builds the Mojo compiler and standard library from source.

Compare how other projects frame openness: Kimi K3.1 Pro's promised open weights and Reflection's Beam release under Apache show how model licenses differ from runtime licenses. The same questions apply on the local side, for example llama.cpp-based Windows apps , which sit on a very permissive stack. On hardware diversity, see Cerebras CS-4 for the kind of non-GPU target a portable compiler tries to reach.

## What are developers likely to ask?

Does "source available" change anything for contributors? Yes, in a practical way. Because the license lets you publish modified source in a fork of Modular's official repository to contribute upstream, pull requests are welcome, but a private fork you distribute as a competing product is not. The repo also ships contribution guidelines and an AI tool policy file, which suggests Modular expects agent-assisted contributions and wants them disclosed.

Is it a timeline of steady opening or a sudden flip? Steady. The README dates show the standard library in March 2024, kernels and GPU abstractions in May 2025, the Python framework in November 2025, the Mojo compiler in August 2026, and now the compiler and runtime for MAX in October 2026. Each step moved the line of what stays closed, and the license wording changed one day before this release.

Will Mojo and MAX diverge on licensing? Possibly. Mojo sits on a plain Apache 2.0 with LLVM Exceptions footing, while MAX mixes two licenses. If you only need the language, the simpler license applies.

## What is still unconfirmed

- Qualcomm's role. The license calls Modular a Qualcomm company. Modular's blog index lists "Qualcomm to Acquire Modular" (June 24, 2026) and "Qualcomm Completes Acquisition of Modular" (July 29, 2026). We do not describe the deal terms.

- Performance and hardware support. The announcement lists CPUs and GPUs. We found no new benchmark numbers tied to the opening, so we are not comparing speed.

- Exact component boundaries. The README says "portions" of MAX use the MAX License. Which directories carry it is indicated by per-file headers and the Licenses folder; check the specific files you depend on.

- Lattner's phrase. The "fully open" line is a social post. It is a fair shorthand for "you can read, change and commercially use it", but not a license term.

## How to check it yourself

- Read LICENSE and Licenses/MAX_LICENSE in the modular/modular repository .

- Open the MAX release list to confirm v26.7 and the changelog.

- Read the October 22 posts on modular.com/blog .

- Grep for license headers in the directories you will touch, since Apache and MAX License files can sit side by side.

Details are accurate as of October 23, 2026, based on Modular's blog index, docs and public repository. Licenses change; read the current file before shipping.
